newsitem.title: USA: Planetary remnants give clue to young solar system.
newsitem.headline: Planetary remnants give clue to young solar system.

text.p: Tiny planet-like bodies at the edge of our solar system may give new clues to what Earth's celestial neighbourhood was like in its infancy, scientists reported on Thursday.
These so-called planetessimals, made up of some of the same kinds of cosmic dust and ice that form the nucleus of comets, are located in a wide band known as the Kuiper belt.

The belt was identified in 1951, but only in the last four years have scientists had the instruments powerful enough to do more than guess at what the planetessimals are made of, researchers said in the latest edition of the journal Science.
These mysterious objects may be as close as scientists can get to the primitive materials that formed the outer planets, Robert Brown of the University of Arizona at Tucson said by telephone.
Held in orbit around the sun but not affected by the gravitational pull of big planets like Jupiter, objects in the Kuiper belt were what was left over after the other planets coalesced, Brown said.

"These objects have stayed in these orbits since the very formation of the solar system," Brown said. "They've sat in this deep freeze for 4.5 billion years or so. They are probably the best sample of the primitive material out of which the solar system formed."
